name: Nora Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for speaking with me, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Lane and Co, a mid-sized agency in a town that's growing because of a big new housing estate on the north side. Three days a week I sit in the show home on the estate selling new-builds for the developer, and two days I'm in the high-street office doing resales. I use AI all day: it drafts my emails, summarises the survey reports and turns my phone videos into tidy walk-through tours. My manager, Pat, calls me the gadget girl.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the show-home days, honestly, because people walk in excited. What drains me is the chain of buyers and sellers falling apart three weeks before completion, and spending a whole day on the phone trying to hold it together. My partner Sami is a chef, so his hours are late and his pay is about the same as mine, which isn't much. We rent a one-bed and have maybe three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, and that's fine. I'd post one of my video tours and say look, this took ten minutes instead of two hours. People in the trade would ask how I did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I've got a small edge and not much more. My job's fine, the estate has another four years of building. But my pay doesn't move just because I'm quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and start selling video tours to two or three smaller agencies, maybe fifty a property. I'd ask Pat if I could do the tours for the whole office for a bit extra. That's real money for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI a lot. Does anything change for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes, I'd just be the quick one. The danger is I get more work dumped on me because I'm fast, without more pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three weeks saved. What's the pressure there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sami's restaurant had a bad winter last year and cut his hours for two months. We lived on my wage and it was tight, really tight. So even with nothing changing I'd want a second income.

I'd post a **video tour** that took ten minutes instead of two hours.
think: I'd have a **small edge** but no rise in pay.
My job is **fine**, with four more years of building on the estate.
do: Sell **video tours** to smaller agencies for about fifty a property.
Ask Pat to pay **a bit extra** for doing the whole office's tours.
feel: She feels **fine** but **impatient**, liking things to move.

fieldNote: Nora's job is **secure for now**, tied to the estate's build-out.

She turns her AI skill into **side money** straight away.

steps.text: Sell AI-edited video tours to smaller agencies
Keep running emails and survey summaries through AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get good at the tools, not to hide from them. I'd probably run a little lunchtime session for the office. Some of them would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of this, mostly. The show-home selling is face-to-face, and I'm already the one who knows the tools. But the resale side would shrink, and Pat would cut someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the follow-ups and paperwork for the show home so I can handle more buyers. I'd keep the video tour side business and push it harder. And I'd look at whether the developer would hire me directly, because that might be safer than the agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle at Lane and Co?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev in the office, who's sixty and does it all on paper. My colleague Kev is lovely and he knows every street, but the resale admin is his whole job. I'd hate to see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the developer still need you in the show home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. People spending that much money still want a face. But the developer's head office would want fewer of us, and I'd want to be the one they keep.

think: I'm mostly on the **right side** of this change.
The **resale side** would shrink and Pat would cut someone.

fieldNote: She sees herself as a **likely winner** in this world.

steps.text: Automate show-home follow-ups and paperwork with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and the government isn't ready. I'd tell people to save what they can, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my edge is gone overnight. If AI can do any thinking work, it can sell a new-build on a website with a perfect virtual tour. The show home might keep one person for keys and coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every penny out of the video tour business in the first year, because it'll vanish too. I'd look at jobs that need a person in the room, maybe hospitality with Sami or care work. We'd cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My whole plan was being the one who's good with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical side of my job is showing people round, and you don't need a robot for that, just an open door and a screen. So the three years doesn't save me much. It saves Sami more, he's in a kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nights out first, then the phone contracts, then the car. We'd keep the flat as long as we could.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and the government **isn't ready**.
I'd tell people to **save** what they can and not panic.
think: My **AI edge** would be gone overnight.
A website with a **virtual tour** could sell new-builds without me.
do: Earn all I can from **video tours** in the first year before they vanish.
Look for **in-person work**, like hospitality or care, and cut spending hard.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, because her plan relied on her AI skills.
S2.quote: My whole plan was being the one who's good with AI.
fieldNote: Like other early adopters, she loses her **edge** when AI runs itself.
She sees **Sami's kitchen job** as safer than hers for now.
Her cuts follow a clear order: **nights out**, phones, then the car.

steps.text: Sell as many video tours as possible in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, and the smart move is to learn something hands-on alongside the tech. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could make the move in time. I'd be thirty-two, with five years to build something that needs a person. The worry is still money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in interior design and home staging, which is hands-on and gets the robot gap. I'd save a hundred a month from the tour money. By year three I'd be staging show homes for developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year of the five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the course for January and open the savings account the same week. Then I'd tell Pat so she can give me show-home days that fit around the classes. Nothing dramatic, just getting it moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a job you'd love to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Staging homes, actually. Staging homes means making a house look like somewhere you'd want to live. I've done it for my own listings for years, moving the sofa, buying a cheap plant, opening the blinds.

say: I'd say the smart move is to learn something **hands-on** alongside the tech.
I'd say we have **a few years** to do it.
think: I could make the move **in time**, at thirty-two, if I start now.
My real worry is still **money**, with three weeks saved and rent due.
do: Start a part-time **home staging** course in January.
Save **a hundred** a month from the video tour money.
S3.quote: Staging homes means making a house look like somewhere you'd want to live.
fieldNote: She picks **home staging** because it's hands-on and gets the robot gap.
Her plan builds on what she **already does** for her own listings.
She still expects to lose her **sales job**.

steps.text: Start a part-time home staging and interior design course
Save a hundred a month from tour income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make a real switch. I'd encourage people to start small now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. I'd sell houses for a few more years, build up the staging business, and move across when it makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling at Lane and Co and use the tools to stay ahead. I'd build the staging side slowly, a few jobs a month. And I'd do the course properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little worry about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes them less rushed. I'd actually enjoy the next few years in the show home instead of counting down. And Sami and I could save before anything big hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start saving earlier. I've spent five years being clever with gadgets and I've got three weeks of money in the bank.

I'd encourage people to **start small** now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge disappears and we have nothing saved. What would help is a bit of money to start the staging business and a course that fits around work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. When both of you are on low pay in different trades, you're always guessing whose job goes first.

She uses AI **every day** and sells video tours on the side.
She's **pragmatic** and calm in slow worlds but alarmed by fast AGI.
She'd move into **home staging**, a hands-on skill she already uses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because her edge vanishes with no savings.
